title: Woe to Those at Ease in Zion
summary: Amos pronounces woe on the comfortable elite of Samaria and Jerusalem, who lounge on ivory beds, feast, drink, and sing while the nation is breaking apart. Because they do not grieve over the ruin of Joseph, they will be the first into exile. God swears by himself that he detests Jacob's pride, and he announces a nation that will oppress Israel from one end of its territory to the other.
story: Amos, a herdsman from Tekoa in Judah, has been preaching in the northern kingdom of Israel during a season of military success and prosperity. Chapter 5 ended with a warning of exile beyond Damascus and a woe on those who long for the Day of the LORD without realizing it will be darkness. Chapter 6 adds a second woe, aimed not at religion this time but at luxury and complacency. It is the last extended speech of judgment before the visions of chapters 7 to 9, and it gathers up themes already sounded: the ivory houses (3:15), the wine drinking (4:1), the corruption of justice (5:7). What is new here is the portrait of a ruling class so comfortable that it cannot feel the disaster coming.
historical:
Amos preached in the reign of Jeroboam II of Israel (about 793 to 753 BC; scholars' dates vary by a few years), when Israel had recovered territory in the north and east. According to 2 Kings 14:25, Jeroboam restored Israel's border "from Lebo-hamath to the Sea of the Arabah". Amos 6:14 turns that very phrase into a threat: the nation God raises up will oppress Israel "from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of the Arabah". The towns Lo-debar and Karnaim (verse 13) lay east of the Jordan in Gilead and Bashan and were probably among the places Jeroboam's armies recaptured from the Arameans. The unnamed nation is almost certainly Assyria, which under Tiglath-pileser III (about 745 to 727 BC) began a series of campaigns that ended with the fall of Samaria in 722 BC.

Verse 2 names three cities: Calneh and Hamath in Syria and Gath in Philistia. The logic of the verse is debated. Some read it as Amos saying, look at these kingdoms that have already fallen; are you any better? Since Assyria took Calneh and Hamath in the 730s and 720s and Gath was conquered later, some scholars think the verse was updated after Amos's time. Others read it as the leaders' own boast (are those kingdoms better than you?), or note that these cities had suffered earlier defeats that Amos's hearers would know. Readers should hold the exact reference loosely.
cultural:
The details of verses 4 to 6 describe a recognizable institution. Excavators at Samaria found hundreds of carved ivory plaques, many of them once fitted to furniture, from roughly this period, and 1 Kings 22:39 speaks of Ahab's ivory house. Eating lambs and stall-fattened calves meant eating meat regularly, a rare luxury in a world where most people ate meat only at festivals. Wine drunk from bowls (the word is used elsewhere for the large bowls of the altar) and the finest oils for anointing the body complete the picture of wealth on display.

The word translated "feasting" in verse 7 is marzeah, known from texts at Ugarit and elsewhere as a kind of banqueting association with its own members, meetings, and sometimes links to funerary or memorial rites. Jeremiah 16:5 uses it for a house of mourning. Amos may be describing such a drinking club of the elite. The irony is sharp if the marzeah had associations with mourning: these people keep a mourning-feast but do not mourn over the real ruin of Joseph. Verses 9 and 10 picture the aftermath of siege or plague: a relative comes to burn or dispose of the dead and silences a survivor from even speaking the LORD's name, perhaps from fear that naming God would draw more of his judgment.
literary: The chapter opens with the Hebrew cry hoy, "woe", the lament raised over the dead, which Amos pronounces over people who are still alive and feasting. Verses 1 to 7 form one sweeping description (you lie, you lounge, you dine, you improvise, you drink, you anoint) that ends in a sudden reversal: those who are "foremost" and anoint themselves with the "finest" oils will go into exile as the "first" of the captives; all three translate forms of the same Hebrew root for first or head. Verses 8 to 11 give a divine oath and a grim scene. Verses 12 to 14 use absurd questions (do horses gallop on cliffs, does anyone plow the sea with oxen?) to expose how unnatural it is to turn justice into poison, and then pun on two place names. Lo-debar sounds like "nothing", and Karnaim means "horns", a symbol of strength. Israel rejoices over Nothing and boasts that it took Horns by its own strength.

outline.t: Woe to the secure leaders of Zion and Samaria
Ivory beds and bowls of wine: the first into exile
God's oath against Jacob's pride and the silence of the dead
Justice turned to poison and a nation raised up

doctrines.note: God's judgment falls first on those who have benefited most from injustice. The leaders who are foremost in privilege become first in exile, a pattern of fitting judgment that runs through the prophets.

The chapter names a sin that is easy to miss because it looks like nothing: comfort that has become indifference. The indictment is not that they enjoy music and food but that they "fail to grieve over the ruin of Joseph" (verse 6).

The LORD swears by himself (verse 8), because there is nothing greater to swear by. His holiness sets him against pride, the self-sufficient boast of verse 13: "Did we not take Karnaim by our own strength?"

words.note: Hoy, woe. A cry of grief used at funerals (1 Kings 13:30 uses it over a dead prophet). When prophets use it, they are singing a lament in advance over people whose way of life has already doomed them. Its use here makes the banquet a funeral.

Marzeah, banquet. Found only here and in Jeremiah 16:5 in the Bible, the word names a feasting association known from other ancient texts. It suggests an organized club of the wealthy rather than an occasional party, and its links to mourning rites sharpen Amos's irony.

Ga'on, pride or majesty. The same word can describe God's majesty in a good sense, and in 8:7 God swears by "the Pride of Jacob". Here it is the arrogance that God says he abhors (verse 8): confidence in citadels and strength rather than in God.

christ: The link to Christ here is thematic. Amos condemns leaders who do not grieve over the ruin of their people. Jesus did the opposite: he wept over Jerusalem as he saw the disaster coming (Luke 19:41-44). His parable of the rich man who dressed in fine linen and feasted every day while Lazarus lay at his gate (Luke 16:19-31) reads like a New Testament echo of Amos 6, and he warned more than once that those who are first will be last. Paul describes Christ as the one who, though rich, became poor for the sake of others (2 Corinthians 8:9), the reverse of the elite of Samaria, who grew rich by making others poor.

hard.q: Is Amos condemning wealth, music, and feasting as such?
hard.a: Not as such. The Old Testament elsewhere celebrates feasts, wine, oil, and music as good gifts of God (Psalm 104:15, Deuteronomy 14:26), and David's music is honored. Amos's target is a particular combination: luxury gained through injustice (see 5:11-12 and 8:4-6), enjoyed in complacency ("You dismiss the day of calamity", verse 3), and indifferent to the suffering of the nation. Some interpreters emphasize the injustice behind the wealth; others emphasize the numbness the wealth produced. Both are in the text. The chapter asks not whether a person may ever enjoy good things but whether their enjoyment has made them unable to see or feel what is happening to others.

questions: Amos says the leaders "fail to grieve over the ruin of Joseph". What losses in your community or nation are easy for comfortable people to ignore, and what would grieving over them look like?
Israel boasted that it took Karnaim (Horns) by its own strength. Where are you tempted to credit your security or success to yourself?
Why might comfort, rather than open wickedness, be one of the most dangerous conditions for a person or a church?
